profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-size SaaS company between the Engineering Research Program Manager and a Senior Data Engineer to scope an internal bibliometric dashboard and briefing note on agile software development research. The company wants to extend a published 2010-2016 bibliometric study through 2024 so engineering leadership can cite current publication trends, major venues, and common study types during an upcoming process-improvement offsite. The agenda is to decide the data collection approach, cleaning and classification steps, division of work, and the timeline for a first reviewable draft. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for assembling the publication corpus, producing the initial charts and venue tables, and setting a Friday checkpoint.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Empirical software engineering, literature synthesis, developer productivity reporting
members.background: Former PhD researcher in software analytics who now leads evidence-based internal studies for the engineering organization and regularly translates academic findings into executive-facing summaries.
members.private_state: She wants the update to look methodologically solid enough to be reused in a future external whitepaper, so she is quietly optimizing for defensible corpus construction and interpretable charts rather than raw speed.
hidden_assumptions: A 'deduplicated dataset' means one canonical record per paper across all databases, with DOI and title normalization resolving cross-source duplicates before any analysis.
When someone says 'the Scopus export,' they mean a fresh, purpose-built export for this study using the agreed search string and document-type filters, not an older exploratory file.
To 'classify study type' means labeling only the final screened agile-relevant papers into categories such as literature review, qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods.
A 'Friday review' is only useful if the trend charts and venue rankings are based on the screened corpus and obvious metadata anomalies have already been checked.

members.name: Lucas Meyer
members.expertise: ETL pipelines, metadata normalization, API-based ingestion, analytics notebooks
members.background: Backend-focused engineer who built the company's internal publication-ingestion tooling and often supports analytics projects by turning semi-structured exports into reproducible datasets and dashboards.
members.private_state: He wants to minimize manual work and prove that the existing ingestion pipeline can support research-style reporting with only light human intervention, so he is quietly steering toward automation-first execution.
hidden_assumptions: A 'deduplicated dataset' means import-level duplicate rows are removed so each source export is clean, while cross-database record merging can wait until later if needed.
When someone refers to 'the Scopus export,' they mean the latest CSV already sitting in the shared project folder unless a new pull is explicitly requested.
To 'classify study type' means adding labels algorithmically across the retrieved records using abstract and keyword rules, with manual review only for edge cases.
A 'Friday review' means the pipeline runs end-to-end and produces draft charts that are directionally correct, even if screening and hand-cleanup are still in progress.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a deduplicated dataset
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to work from a 'deduplicated dataset.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means a paper-level corpus where the same article appearing in Scopus and Web of Science has already been collapsed into one canonical record.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means duplicate rows from the same import have been removed, while the same paper can still exist as separate records from different sources.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using familiar data-pipeline language that usually signals good hygiene, so the phrase sounds fully aligned and neither expects that the other attaches a different granularity to 'duplicate.'

misalignment_points.topic: Which Scopus export they plan to use
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to starting from 'the Scopus export' or 'the baseline export.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of a new export to be pulled for this project using the final query, covering 2010-2024 and including both journal articles and conference papers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the existing shared-drive Scopus CSV from a prior exploratory run, which is limited to 2010-2023 and uses a journal-heavy filter.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team has only one obviously named Scopus file in the folder and both assume that the artifact they have in mind is the common reference point, so the phrase feels specific enough even though it is not.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the study-type classification task
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that they need to 'classify study type.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes classification happens after relevance screening and applies only to the final included agile software development papers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes classification is a broad enrichment step applied to all retrieved records before or alongside screening so the pipeline can summarize everything automatically.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Classification sounds like a straightforward metadata step, and both parties are focused on sequencing work rather than explicitly restating the corpus boundary that classification should attach to.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the Friday review ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on having a 'first cut ready for Friday review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks Friday review readiness means stakeholder-facing charts and tables are already based on the screened, cleaned corpus and are stable enough to discuss substantive findings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks Friday review readiness means there is a working draft output from the pipeline, even if some charts still reflect pre-screening counts and pending cleanup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'first cut' naturally implies an early draft to both people, but each silently uses a different quality threshold for what counts as reviewable in a planning context.

turns.inner_thought: We need something leadership can cite confidently at the offsite, but I also want this to stand up as a reusable evidence asset later. Extending the 2010-2016 study through 2024 means we need a clean, defensible corpus and charts that won't fall apart under scrutiny. A first cut for Friday review only helps me if the counts and venue tables are already grounded in the screened set and obvious metadata issues are handled.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The goal is pretty straightforward: extend that published agile bibliometric study from 2010 through 2024 so leadership has an updated view for the process-improvement offsite. I'd like us to have a first cut ready for Friday review, and today I want to nail down the collection approach, cleanup steps, and who owns what.

turns.inner_thought: This is a good chance to show the ingestion stack can handle research reporting without a bunch of handwork. Fastest path is to start from the Scopus CSV already sitting in the shared folder from the exploratory pass and push that through the pipeline today. If we can get draft outputs by Friday, that's enough to prove the flow works end to end.
turns.utterance: Yep, that sounds doable. To save time, I'd start from the baseline export that's already in the project folder and wire the ingestion around that, then we can layer the rest on top instead of rebuilding everything from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he is aligned on beginning with the Scopus export for this study. Once that fresh pull is in place with the agreed query and year range through 2024, I want Web of Science added so we aren't overfitting to one index. The original study had a broad venue picture, and leadership will notice if conference-heavy agile work is missing.
turns.utterance: That works for me. Once the Scopus export is in place, I'd definitely want Web of Science layered in as well so the corpus tracks the broader venue picture from the original study rather than leaning too heavily on a single source.

turns.inner_thought: I can clean each import quickly before charting. For me the key is to remove duplicate rows inside the source files first so the trend line isn't inflated by ingestion noise; if the same paper shows up in multiple databases, we can reconcile that after we see whether it materially changes anything. No need to slow down the first pass.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I'll get us to a deduplicated dataset before I generate the charts, so the yearly trend line is at least straightforward from the start.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Once we've collapsed cross-source duplicates into one canonical paper-level record, then we can classify study type on the actual included agile corpus. I need those labels to support a defensible narrative about whether review papers still dominate and how qualitative versus quantitative work has shifted over time.
turns.utterance: Great. After deduplication, we should classify study type so we can say something useful about whether literature reviews still dominate and whether qualitative and quantitative work are staying in roughly the same balance.

turns.inner_thought: That part should be easy to automate. I can infer study type from abstracts, author keywords, maybe title cues, and run it across everything we retrieve so the dashboard has coverage immediately. If there are edge cases, Priya can spot-check later, but I don't want classification waiting on manual screening.
turns.utterance: Yeah, classify study type should be pretty automatable. I can drive that off abstracts and keywords and push labels through the full retrieved set as part of the pipeline, then we can clean up edge cases if anything looks off.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep emphasizing the leadership-facing outputs. The top venues need to be stable and human-readable, not a noisy list split across metadata variants. If this is going to end up in a briefing note and maybe later a whitepaper, I need journals and conferences normalized cleanly enough that nobody questions the rankings.
turns.utterance: One thing I'd put a little extra care on is the venue side. I especially want the main journals and conferences called out cleanly, because leadership is very likely to quote the top venues directly when they talk about where this research is landing.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. The pipeline can output counts by venue and year quickly, even if some source cleanup remains. For Friday, I just need something directionally solid: publication counts, venue rankings, study-type charts. We can always tighten normalization and filtering after the checkpoint instead of blocking on perfection.
turns.utterance: Understood. What I can aim for is a first cut for Friday review with publication counts, venue rankings, and method-type charts, and then we can tighten anything noisy after we look at it together.

turns.inner_thought: That should work as long as Friday's package is already based on the screened, cleaned corpus rather than raw retrieval. Once the dataset is genuinely deduplicated across sources and the study-type labels are attached to the included papers, I can spot-check a sample and start drafting the narrative over the weekend. That keeps us on track for something I can stand behind externally if needed.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll plan to spot-check a sample once the dataset is deduplicated and the study-type labels are attached, and if that looks stable enough I can start drafting the narrative over the weekend.

turns.inner_thought: Great, we're aligned. I'll use the Scopus export that's already there today, add Web of Science after that, run dedupe and classification through the pipeline, and post whatever the system produces for Friday. This should be a nice demonstration that the existing tooling can support this kind of analysis with very little manual intervention.
